beginner: Oregano likes soil that is neutral to a little bit chalky, about pH 6.5 to 7.5, and copes anywhere from 6.0 to 8.0. It does not do well in acidic soil, so if your soil is sour, a small amount of garden lime nudges it where oregano wants it.

beginner: The trick with oregano is to not fuss over it. Give it the sunniest, best-draining spot you have, water it only when the soil dries out, and do not feed it much. beginner: There are several kinds of oregano. Greek oregano is the bold, spicy one used in cooking and sold dried, and it is the best choice for the kitchen. Italian oregano is milder and sweeter. Common or wild oregano is the toughest and most cold-hardy, but its flavor varies a lot and some plants are almost bland, so taste it first. Hot & Spicy is extra strong, Golden oregano has bright yellow leaves, and Syrian oregano is the za'atar herb. Watch out for one thing: Mexican oregano is a completely different plant (in the verbena family), not a true oregano, even though it tastes similar. For cooking, start with Greek oregano.
seasoned: Oregano reaches the grower as several practical types. Greek oregano (Origanum vulgare subsp. hirtum) is the hot, pungent kitchen standard and the type sold dried; Italian oregano (O. x majoricum, an oregano-marjoram hybrid) is milder and sweeter. Common or wild oregano (O. vulgare) is the hardiest and most vigorous but has variable, sometimes bland flavor, so taste before you rely on it. Hot & Spicy is an extra-pungent selection, Golden oregano (O. vulgare 'Aureum') is a bright-foliaged ornamental-culinary form, and Syrian oregano (O. syriacum) is the tender za'atar herb. One important caution: Mexican oregano (Lippia graveolens) is not a true oregano at all but a shrub in the verbena family, grown in hot climates for a similar, stronger flavor. For cooking, start with Greek oregano.

beginner: Try not to feed it. Oregano needs very little, and too much fertilizer gives soft leaves with less flavor. The same is true for water, where more is not better.

beginner: Once it is established, snip oregano often. Regular cutting keeps it bushy and slows it turning woody, and you can pick leaves anytime to cook with.

seasoned: Cut out old, leggy wood in early spring once growth resumes and frost has passed, and pull up any shoots that have crept beyond where you want them. Cutting into leafy growth, not bare old wood, gives the best regrowth.

seasoned: For the strongest flavor, harvest and cut for drying just as the flower buds form, before they open, when the leaf oils peak. Pinch or cut off the flowers to favor leaf growth and keep the best flavor.

beginner: Decide about the flowers. Cutting them off keeps the leaves tasting best and stops the plant spreading by seed; leaving a few for the bees is fine, but snip them before they make seed.

beginner: Trim off the old flowers before they make seed. Oregano drops a lot of seed and can pop up all over, so deadheading it as you cut back keeps the seedlings down.
seasoned: Deadhead as you shear to limit self-seeding. Oregano seeds readily and can sow itself across a bed, so cutting the spent flowers before seed matures keeps stray seedlings down.

beginner: Oregano is a low, spreading herb with pungent, fragrant leaves you cook with, famous on pizza and in tomato sauces. It comes from the dry Mediterranean, so it wants full sun, poor dry soil, and very little water, and it does worse if you pamper it. It grows about 1 to 2 feet tall in a bushy mound. The leaves taste best just before it flowers in mid-to-late summer, so many gardeners pinch off the flowers, and oregano is one of the few herbs that tastes even stronger dried. It is tough and rarely bothered by pests, but it spreads by creeping roots and dropped seed, so it is best grown in a pot or with edging. Watch out: Mexican oregano is a different plant, not true oregano.
seasoned: Oregano is a spreading, low, woody Mediterranean perennial in the mint family, grown for its pungent aromatic leaves that flavor pizza, tomato sauces, meats, and Mediterranean and Mexican dishes. It forms a bushy, mat-like mound about 1 to 2 feet tall and thrives on neglect in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; wet, rich, or humid conditions rot it and dull its flavor. Its flavor peaks just before its mid-to-late-summer bloom, so many growers pinch off the flowers to keep the leaves at their best, and the leaves are unusual in tasting even stronger dried. It is hardy and pest-resistant but spreads by creeping stems and self-sown seed, so it is best contained. Note that Mexican oregano is a different, unrelated plant.

Pinching or cutting off the flowers keeps the leaves pungent, and regular harvesting keeps the plant bushy. Oregano is one of the few herbs whose flavor deepens when dried.

Most types are reliable in roughly zones 5 to 9, with zone 3 grown as an annual or a bring-in container plant, and tender types like Syrian oregano hardy only in the warmest zones.
